title: Is the straight line the fastest?
hook: Running is fast, swimming is slow. Where should a lifeguard hit the water?

knows: lifeguards run on sand and swim in water

misconception: The fastest route is always the straight line.
objective: The learner can explain that when speeds differ on two sides of a boundary, the quickest path bends there, and that light refracts for the same reason.

claims.text: With the lifeguard 40 m up the beach, the swimmer 20 m out and 60 m along, the straight line crosses the shore at 40 m and takes 26.9 s at 7 m/s running and 1.5 m/s swimming.
Entering at 56 m takes 23.4 s, the fastest of the stage's 8 m steps; the true best entry is 56.4 m.
At the fastest entry point, sin(angle on sand)/7 equals sin(angle in water)/1.5.
claims.source: dt/dx = 0 gives (x / r1)/v1 = ((60 - x)/r2)/v2, i.e. sin(a1)/v1 = sin(a2)/v2 with angles from the normal. At x = 56.45: 0.1166 vs 0.1165.

claims.text: Light takes the quickest path between two points (Fermat's principle) and travels slower in water than in air, so its path bends where it enters the water: refraction.
claims.source: Fermat's principle and its derivation of Snell's law; Feynman Lectures on Physics, vol. I, ch. 26; Hecht, Optics, ch. 4.

claims.text: Model: flat beach, straight shoreline, steady running and swimming speeds; drawn to scale.
claims.source: Stated on stage ('Drawn to scale') and in the reveal; speeds are illustrative (brief cm-physics #20).

recall.question: A ray of light goes from air into glass, where it is slower. At the surface it…
options: Goes straight on: straight is fastest
Bends toward the slow side, like the lifeguard swimming less
Bends away so it spends longer in the glass
recall.why: Light takes the least-time path; like the lifeguard, it shortens the slow part, so it bends at the boundary toward the perpendicular in the glass.
